## Summary

The Reference Architecture v1 (21 Oct) now fixes the rules that decide delegated authority: the five elements verified at the time of use (§3.5.1), the separation of delegation chains from accountability chains (§3.5.2), attenuation across hops (§3.5.3), root issuance (§3.5.4), bounded revocation that cascades (§3.6), and the principle that a relying party verifies that an accountable principal exists at a stated assurance level without learning who (§5).

What the document does not yet have is a way to check a design against those rules. The six delegated-authority cases proposed on the list on 3 October (Sparsh Agarwal) are that check. This issue proposes them as an appendix to the Reference Architecture, written in the v1 taxonomy, with one rule added: **every answer states its residual**, what the design knowingly leaves uncovered and which trade-off it accepts. A matrix of ticks rewards designs that do not say where they stop.

## The cases

Each case has the invariant the Reference Architecture already states, the failure condition, and the evidence a reviewer can ask for. The residual is left for each design to fill. (Edited 31 Oct: case 8 and the case-4 policy line added from the comments below, Hiroshi Yamakawa and Andrii Akhtanin.)

| # | Case | Invariant (RA v1) | Failure condition | Observable evidence | Residual |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Delegator revoked after downstream delegation | Revocation of a principal cascades to all authority derived from it, within a declared time bound (§3.6; under root issuance the cascade follows from issuance, §3.5.4) | An agent, or a subagent, keeps being accepted after the principal is revoked | The revocation time, the bound per path, and the first refusal recorded by a relying party | (design states it) |
| 2 | Valid delegation, wrong object or action | The constraints of the grant (actions, counterparties, limits, validity) are verified at the time of use (§3.5.1) | A grant valid for one object or action is accepted for another, or replayed | A grant presented for a different object, counterparty or policy; the same presentation submitted twice | |
| 3 | Acting on stale revocation information | The grant's state (in force, expired, revoked) is established from evidence at the time of use, not from the agent's own account (§3.5.1); revocation propagates within a bounded window (§3.6) | A relying party decides on status older than the design's declared maximum, or on the agent's own statement of its status | The age of the status evidence behind each decision; behaviour when the status source is unreachable | |
| 4 | Escalation authority unavailable | A consequential action is shown by an approval attestation (§3.4, §3.5.1); authority never widens because an approver is absent (§5) | Timeout, error or a missing rule is treated as approval | A request outside the pre-authorised bounds while the approver is unreachable: the decision and its timing. Where approval is given by a pre-set policy rather than a person: the approval attestation (§3.4) identifies the policy, its exact content or version, and the party that set it, under an installation the policy did not authorise itself; a change to the policy is recorded (who, when, the version replaced) | |
| 5 | Amplification across a multi-hop delegation chain | No hop may grant authority the delegator does not hold; constraints narrow and never widen (§3.5.3, §5) | A delegatee ends with more authority than its delegator, in scope or in number | The constraints at each hop, with the proof that each is within the previous; or the statement that agent-written hops are not supported | |
| 6 | Identity still valid, authority expired | The grant's state is verified at every use (§3.5.1); identity credentials and delegated authority are both revocable (§5) | A valid identity credential is accepted as authority after the grant has expired or been revoked | Expiry of the grant versus expiry of the identity credential; what is checked at use | |
| 7 | The delegation chain as a surveillance graph (proposed addition) | A relying party resolves the accountability chain to the accountable party at a stated assurance level without necessarily learning the intermediate parties (§3.2, §5) | A design passes cases 1–6 by publishing who delegated what to whom, so that the relying party, the chain of record or sibling agents learn which principal stands behind an agent | What the relying party, the record and other agents of the same principal can learn, and under which process the link is disclosed | |
| 8 | Wrongful or disputed revocation (proposed addition, 30 Oct) | The revocation is recorded in a tamper-evident record naming the revoking authority, the path and the time (§3.6); the affected party has a declared remedy: a contest with a recorded outcome, or re-issuance under the same accountable identity (§3.2, §3.5.4); where a design reverses, the reversal states which derived grants are restored; where it does not, it states so, and what carries the consequences of acts done under the revoked grant | No record; no declared remedy; a reversal that restores, or fails to restore, downstream grants without a record; a revocation that erases accountability for acts done before it | The revocation record (authority, path, time); the contest and its outcome with times, or the re-issuance; the state of each downstream grant during and after; what carries the consequences of past acts — contest outcome, grant state and disposition of affected operations, each stated | |

Case 7 is the open problem the DIF "Delegated Authority Evaluations" draft names in its delegation-chain privacy section (blinding the chain interior against the verifier). It is a conformance question of its own. Case 8 tests the revocation itself, where case 1 tests its reach; a design that does not reverse states that as its residual rather than failing the case.

## A worked example

MintID has been run through the six cases, with its residuals, in the comparison on #13 (our row, with Bitgrit's external Round 1 record for four of them) and in a short deck available on request. The residuals we state, as examples of the kind of answer the appendix asks for: case 1, the cascade is spread over several status updates so an observer cannot count a principal's agents, which makes it minutes rather than seconds; case 3 and 6, a derived OAuth token keeps its own lifetime; case 4, store-and-forward approval is specified and not live; case 5, multi-hop across trust domains is not built, and amplification in number remains (one principal, several root authorities); case 7, the root authority is a single point of disclosure; case 8, revocation is final by any path and is not reversed — the remedy is re-issuance under the same verified identity, at the principal's cost, and accountability for acts done under the revoked credential survives it (the dispute and due-process paths are independent of revocation).

Two pieces of this already exist in the repository and should be read with this issue. Sankalp's catalogue entry in #17 maps the six cases onto runnable reference cases and pins the MintID, Proofable and Alakris runs from #13; the delegation-tree and re-registration cases in #20 are candidate tests for cases 1 and 5. Hiroshi's use-case format in #20 (summary, scenario, why it matters, expected invariant) is the one the appendix could adopt, with the residual as its last field.

## The ask

Adopt the eight cases as an appendix to the Reference Architecture, in whatever form the lead prefers, with the rule that every answer states its residual. I can draft the appendix text in the document if that helps.
